summary: Psalm 55 begins with a desperate plea for God to listen as the speaker describes fear, oppression, and a longing to escape. The danger is not only from enemies in the city but from a companion and familiar friend who has betrayed trust. The psalm moves from panic and accusation toward repeated prayer, a call to cast one's burden on Yahweh, and a final statement of trust.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows how the Psalter makes room for fear, betrayal, anger, and trust in the same prayer. It also gives a clear example of a lament that asks God for judgment while refusing to present the speaker as calm or detached.

context.author: The heading associates the psalm with David, but Psalms is an anthology and such headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or collection; their exact historical force is debated.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, later used by Jewish and Christian communities in public prayer and private life.
context.date: Individual psalms come from different periods, and the final five-book Psalter is a later anthology; this chapter should not be assigned one certain date from this chapter alone.
context.setting: The poem speaks from an unnamed crisis involving enemies, violence in a city, and betrayal by a close companion.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic lament and prayer, with a musical heading and Selah markers preserved in the text.

outline.heading: Urgent Plea And Inner Distress
outline.note: The speaker asks God to listen and describes oppression, fear, trembling, and the terrors of death.

outline.heading: The Wish To Escape
outline.note: The speaker imagines having wings like a dove and fleeing to a wilderness shelter away from the storm.

outline.heading: Violence In The City
outline.note: The speaker asks God to confuse his opponents because violence, strife, malice, abuse, threats, and lies fill the city.

outline.heading: Betrayal By A Friend
outline.note: The deepest wound is that the offender was a companion who once shared fellowship and worship with the speaker.

outline.heading: Prayer And Confidence
outline.note: The speaker contrasts his own calling on God with opponents who do not change and do not fear God.

outline.heading: Smooth Words, Broken Trust, And Final Appeal
outline.note: The betrayer's friendly speech hides violence, but the psalm urges casting one's burden on Yahweh and ends with trust in God.

keyVerses.text: I said, “Oh that I had wings like a dove! Then I would fly away, and be at rest.
keyVerses.why: This line captures the speaker's desire not to win an argument but to escape overwhelming pressure.

keyVerses.text: But it was you, a man like me, my companion, and my familiar friend.
keyVerses.why: The psalm's crisis sharpens here: the pain comes from betrayal by someone close, not only from an obvious enemy.

keyVerses.text: Evening, morning, and at noon, I will cry out in distress. He will hear my voice.
keyVerses.why: The speaker's distress becomes repeated prayer rather than silence or simple revenge.

keyVerses.text: Cast your burden on Yahweh and he will sustain you. He will never allow the righteous to be moved.
keyVerses.why: This is the psalm's clearest turn toward trust, while still standing inside a chapter full of threat and betrayal.

themes: Violence and deceit in the city

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading says, “A contemplation by David,” so the received text associates the psalm with David. Psalm headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging, so readers differ on how directly to treat this as a biographical notice. The poem itself gives a first-person speaker in distress, betrayed by someone close.

questions.question: What kind of trouble is the speaker facing?
questions.answer: The speaker describes enemy voices, wicked oppression, suffering, anger, and deathly fear. Later verses add violence and strife in the city, along with threats and lies in its streets. The chapter does not name a specific historical event, so it is safest to describe the crisis in the poem's own terms.

questions.question: Why does the speaker wish for wings like a dove?
questions.answer: The image expresses a desire to flee and find rest, not a claim that escape has actually happened. The speaker imagines wandering far off, lodging in the wilderness, and hurrying to shelter from storm. It is a poetic picture of exhaustion under pressure.

questions.question: What does “Selah” mean here?
questions.answer: The chapter preserves “Selah” after verse 7 and again in verse 19. It is an uncertain musical or performance marker whose exact instruction is no longer known. It signals that the psalm has a performance history, but its exact use at these points cannot be reconstructed from the text.

questions.question: Why is the betrayal worse than ordinary hostility?
questions.answer: The speaker says the insult did not come from an enemy or from someone who openly hated him. It came from “my companion, and my familiar friend,” someone who had shared fellowship and gone to God's house with him. The pain is intensified because trust and worshiping companionship have been violated.

questions.question: Is the familiar friend certainly Ahithophel?
questions.answer: Some later readers have connected these verses with Ahithophel because David's story includes a counselor who turned against him. Psalm 55 itself does not name Ahithophel, so this remains a possible identification rather than an established fact about the poem.

questions.question: How should a first-time reader understand the harsh requests for judgment?
questions.answer: The psalm asks God to confuse the violent and even says, “Let death come suddenly on them.” That is morally intense language, and readers should not flatten it into polite speech or turn it into permission for private revenge. Within the chapter, the speaker directs the demand to God while naming wickedness, violence, and deceit as the problem.

questions.question: What changes when the speaker says, “As for me”?
questions.answer: Verse 16 marks a contrast between the enemies and the speaker's chosen response. Instead of only describing danger, the speaker says he will call on God and that Yahweh will save him. The following verses continue that turn by describing repeated prayer and confidence that God hears.

questions.question: Does verse 22 erase the pain described earlier in the psalm?
questions.answer: No. “Cast your burden on Yahweh” comes after fear, betrayal, violence, and urgent pleas for judgment have already been voiced. The line gives a trust statement inside distress, not a denial that distress is real. The final verse still speaks of destruction, deceit, and the speaker's trust in God.

glossary.def: A plea or request for help; in verse 1 the speaker asks God not to hide from it.
A preserved performance marker in the psalm; its exact musical or liturgical function is uncertain.
The place of the dead in the language of the psalm; verse 15 uses it in a request for the wicked to go down alive.
The weight or care the speaker tells the hearer to cast on Yahweh in verse 22.
